new_en: (1) In the second blessing. Because it contains resurrection of the dead, and rain sustains life just as resurrection restores life. (2) In the Mussaf prayer, etc. It would have been appropriate to begin mentioning rain on the first Yom Tov of Sukkot, when judgment concerning water takes place. However, rain is a sign of curse during Sukkot because one cannot sit in the sukkah while it rains, so rain is not mentioned until the 7 days of dwelling in the sukkah have passed. Strictly speaking, one should begin immediately on the night of the final Yom Tov, but at Maariv not everyone is in the synagogue, and the congregation would become divided, with some mentioning rain and others not. Why not begin at Shacharit? Some write that an individual may not mention rain until the prayer leader or attendant announces 'Morid hageshem' aloud before the prayer, as explained below, and this cannot be announced at Shacharit because redemption must be joined to the Amidah. See Taz for another reason. If one erred and mentioned 'Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem' at Maariv of Shemini Atzeret or at Shacharit, he does not repeat the prayer. (3) Until the Mussaf prayer. We likewise do not cease mentioning rain from the preceding evening so that the congregation will not be divided. When they cease at Mussaf, everyone knows because the prayer leader or attendant announces 'Morid hatal' before Mussaf, and the announcement of dew signals that the mention of rain is ending. This applies to the Sephardic custom of saying 'Morid hatal' during the summer. In our countries, where 'Morid hatal' is not said in summer, this wording cannot be announced. Nor is it proper to announce explicitly that they should stop saying 'Morid hageshem,' because that appears as though one rejects rain, in keeping with the statement that one does not pray for an excess of goodness. Rama therefore rules in seif 3 that the custom is to continue mentioning rain until Minchah, after everyone has heard the prayer leader omit it in Mussaf. During the silent Mussaf, however, both the congregation and the prayer leader still mention rain, so that the congregation will not be divided. If one erred at Maariv of Pesach, or at Shacharit or Mussaf, and did not mention 'Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem,' all agree that he does not repeat.
Him. Rain is harmful during the summer. Dew. According to the Sephardic custom, in which one says during summer 'Mashiv haruach umorid hatal,' this case means that he said rain in place of dew.

He said 'Morid hageshem,' etc. Since during the summer there is a period when rain is harmful, namely the harvest season, when rain is normally withheld, and this person prays for rain and thereby requests something harmful, he must repeat the prayer throughout the summer.

5) There, in the Mussaf prayer of the final Yom Tov, etc. We do not begin mentioning rain at Maariv because not everyone is in the synagogue and the congregation would become divided, some mentioning it and others not. We do not begin at Shacharit so that a person will not suppose that it had been mentioned the previous evening and then, the following year, begin at night. There is another reason why we do not begin at Shacharit. Rabbi Chaggai bar Padas said that an individual may not mention rain until the prayer leader mentions it, meaning that the prayer leader must say 'Mashiv haruach' aloud before the prayer. This cannot be done at Shacharit because redemption must be joined to the Amidah. So writes the Rosh based on the Yerushalmi, cited by Beit Yosef; Derishah, letter 1; Taz, seif katan 2; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there. The Yerushalmi gives another reason. Rabbi Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yehudah's reason is that the festivals should depart with dew, because dew is beneficial. Rosh explains that this rationale concerns the beginning of the mention rather than its cessation. On Yom Tov everyone comes to the synagogue in the evening, since no melacha is done, so the first reason is insufficient. The arrangement therefore allows dew to be mentioned on the festival also at Maariv and Shacharit. Beit Yosef and Derishah cite this. See the following letter and letter 7.

Seif katan 2, until the prayer, etc. Bach writes, etc., and that must be said, etc. Meaning, if one erred at Shacharit and recited the weekday Amidah until the blessing Barech Aleinu, he should say within Barech Aleinu, 'and give dew and rain.' 'To mention' means saying 'Mashiv haruach,' etc. Regarding requesting rain, etc., as explained above at the beginning of siman 114. In any event, not everyone begins on the first day. The words 'and as stated above, that they departed,' etc., contain a scribal error. The correct text is: Furthermore, according to what Beit Yosef wrote above in siman 114 in the name of the Yerushalmi, Rabbi Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yehudah's reason is that the festivals should depart with dew because dew is beneficial. Even after leaving the sukkah, rainfall on Yom Tov diminishes people's joy, for the heart is happier when the sky is clear and rain is not falling. Rosh explains that this comes to answer why we do not begin requesting rain at Maariv of Shemini Atzeret. The earlier reason in the Yerushalmi, that not everyone is present in synagogue at night, suffices regarding the cessation of the mention at Mussaf on the first day of Pesach because on the preceding evening people are occupied with preparing for Yom Tov, matzah, and maror. On the night of Shemini Atzeret, however, Chol HaMoed preceded it and people are not occupied in this way, so everyone comes to synagogue. One might therefore have expected them to begin at Maariv. The Yerushalmi explains that the festivals should depart with dew, and they did not even wish to mention rain then. This makes Bach's statement that an individual should begin earlier difficult. Nevertheless, the individual follows the congregation. Tur writes in the name of Ra'avyah that the 60 days after the seasonal cycle require complete 24-hour periods. Thus if the tekufah occurred 3 hours into the day, and the congregation prays on the 60th day before those 3 hours have passed, they do not request rain. If an individual later prays after the 3-hour point, when the time of requesting rain has technically arrived, he still follows the congregation, which did not request rain, and does not say 'Veten tal umatar.' Although we do not rule like Ra'avyah regarding the requirement of complete 24-hour periods, there is no disagreement with the principle that in a case of this sort the individual follows the congregation. The same applies here. Darchei Moshe gives another answer, etc. Meaning, how can Bach's position be rejected when proof for it might be drawn from Tur's resolution of Beit Yosef's question? He therefore notes that Darchei Moshe gave another resolution. In order to publicize, etc. Meaning, because there is no announcement that the congregation is ceasing, as Magen Avraham writes in siman 114, seif katan 5, the liturgical poems requesting blessed dew publicize that they are ceasing to request rain. This follows the Sephardic custom of mentioning dew throughout the summer. We Ashkenazim at least at the beginning of summer, during Mussaf on the first day of Pesach, pray for blessed dew. Until those poems are recited it has not yet been publicized that the congregation has ceased mentioning and requesting rain. Tur's wording, 'until Mussaf,' is therefore understandable, because until that point the period of requesting rain appears to continue. One should say 'from Your goodness,' not 'from its goodness.' Maharshal explains that satiation does not come from the goodness of the land, which is a separate blessing. As Rashi explains the verse 'You shall eat your bread to satisfaction' in Parashat Bechukotai, this is an additional blessing: one eats a small amount and it becomes blessed within his stomach.

And the congregation, etc. Amen is answered only after the one who recites the blessing, namely the kohen. The wording here implies that 'Ken yehi ratzon' is said only after the conclusion of Birkat Kohanim. The widespread custom, however, is to say 'Yehi ratzon' after the first 2 blessings and 'Ken yehi ratzon' after the third. A reason may be offered: without peace, nothing is complete, and the third blessing is peace, which completes the principal blessing. Therefore 'Ken yehi ratzon' is said there to indicate that this is the culmination of the blessing. A copy from Sefer Etz Chaim composed by the divine sage Maharam Kalpiras, a disciple of the holy divine sage Rabbi Yitzchak Luria, regarding matters of prayer: After the passage of the Tamid one should recite Pittum HaKetoret. In 'Yayin Kafrisin,' the yud is pronounced with a tzere. The tallis should cover the head tefillin. Whenever one says Ashrei, he should afterward say 'And we shall bless God,' etc. He would not remove his tallis and tefillin until after Aleinu. After Aleinu one should say, 'Hashem shall be King over all the earth; on that day Hashem shall be One and His Name One.' One should have in mind that the verse begins with a vav and ends with a dalet, which together equal 10, corresponding to the 10 sefirot. This is what I saw there. The baraita, 'Our Rabbis taught: Nothing precedes the morning Tamid,' etc., is in Pesachim, chapter Tamid Nishchat, page 59. Tosafos write there that Rabbeinu Yitzchak holds that the word 'lamps' should not be included, because the teaching lists only matters burned upon the altar, regarding which the Torah was particular that they come afterward, as the verse says, 'and he shall burn upon it the fats of the peace offerings.' When reciting the first verse of Shema, 'Hashem is our God, Hashem is One,' one should have in mind the 4 letters of the Divine Name. When saying 'Blessed is the Name of His glorious kingdom,' one should have in mind the 4 letters of the Name of lordship. When saying 'forever and ever,' one should have in mind the combined Name formed from those 2 Divine Names. When saying 'May His great Name be exalted,' one should have in mind that He, blessed is He, rules over the 4 worlds of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah. 'Le'alam,' in the singular, corresponds to Atzilut, where there is great unity. 'Ul'almei' corresponds to Beriah; 'almaya' corresponds to Yetzirah; and 'b'alma' corresponds to Asiyah. When saying 'Yitbarach,' one should bow, since the word contains the root associated with bending the knee, and one also bows at 'Lecha.' In the wording 'He is appeased with mercy and reconciled through supplications,' a new edition printed 'and enticed through supplications.' This is incorrect, because Ramban writes in Parashat Mishpatim, regarding 'If a man entices,' that enticement refers to false words.

In Magen Avraham at the end of seif katan 1. Note: His words require study. Shaar HaMelech already addressed them in chapter 19 of the Laws of Shabbos, and in a responsum I discussed this at length. The primary explanation, in my view, is that one who examines Darchei Moshe will understand the matter correctly without any strain or difficulty. He holds that if there are already kohanim ascending to the duchan, then an Israelite who ascends together with them constitutes hiddur mitzvah through 'in a multitude of people is the King's glory.' Wherever there is hiddur mitzvah, there is no prohibition of adding to a mitzvah, as Rambam writes in chapter 6 of the Laws of Sukkah and Lulav, law 7; see Kesef Mishneh there. The same applies here, and there is no violation of the positive commandment 'Thus shall you bless.' This appears to me to be correct.
